responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character05_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Look, I remember him talking about fairness like it was something real simple but nobody actually followed. He’d say, “Fair don’t mean everybody gets the same thing — fair means you get a shot.” That stuck with me. He grew up in a working-class neighborhood where folks worked hard, maybe two jobs, and still couldn’t get ahead. His dad lost his factory job when he was 18 — got replaced, not by an immigrant, but by a machine. But then he saw other guys, same boat, getting told there weren’t any openings while he’d drive past warehouses hiring workers from out of state, even from other countries, for less pay.

So to him, fairness wasn’t about handouts. It was about playing by the same rules. If you’re here legally, paying taxes, trying to work — you deserve respect. But he also felt like the system bends for some and breaks others. Like, why do rich developers bring in crews from outside when local guys are begging for work? That didn’t sit right.

On belonging… man, that one hit close. He never felt like the country really saw people like him — white, yes, but poor, undereducated, living paycheck to paycheck. He didn’t feel part of the “American dream” crowd on TV. Said he belonged to his block, his crew at the garage, the corner store guy who knew his name. Community, to him, wasn’t flags or slogans — it was showing up. It was knowing your neighbor’s kid needs a ride to practice, or covering a shift when someone’s sick.

He used to say, “You don’t just *join* a community — you *build* it, day by day.” So when people came in — immigrants or not — he judged them by whether they were trying to build *with* us, or just take what they could and leave. Didn’t matter if you were born here or came yesterday — what mattered was: Are you holding up your end?

One time he told me about this Mexican family that moved into the apartment above Mrs. Langston. At first, people whispered — “they don’t speak good English,” “they’ve got too many relatives staying over.” But then the dad started fixing up the building for free — repaired the stairs, painted the hall. The mom watched kids after school. And the son helped old Mr. Dale carry his groceries every week.

Character05_M said, “Now *that’s* belonging. Not where you come from. It’s what you *do.*”

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character05_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*Sitting here in the garden, hands on my knees, sun hitting the back of my neck — I look around and see all kinds.*

I ain’t gonna lie — some folks, at first glance, they throw me off. Like that guy down the path, always smoking something that don’t smell like tobacco, stumbling a little, talking to himself. Used to make me tense. But then one day he helped me pick up groceries when a bag broke. Didn’t have to do it. Did it anyway. Turns out he’s got PTSD from Iraq. Veteran. Same age as me. That changed how I saw him.

Then there’s Maria and her kids — came from Guatemala five years ago. She works cleaning offices downtown, gets home at 10 p.m., still makes sure her daughter does homework at the picnic table right there every night. I’ve seen her shovel snow for old Mrs. Peet next door without being asked. That earns respect.

And yeah, some people live different — couples not married, raising kids together like it’s nothing. Or folks with tattoos head to toe, speaking languages I can’t place. Doesn’t bother me unless they’re bothering someone else.

Thing is, growing up where I did, you learn fast: people are people. Some good, some bad, most just trying to get by. I don’t care if your skin’s brown, black, or purple — what matters is if you treat this block like home or like a pit stop.

I remember one winter, power went out for three days. No heat. This Somali family — the Abdis — fired up their generator, opened their basement. Had space heaters, hot tea, even lent us blankets. Fed half the building. We sat together, cold but laughing, kids playing cards by flashlight. That’s when it hit me — *this* is community. Not bloodlines. Not papers. It’s who shows up when it’s dark and cold.

But — and this is real — I also get nervous sometimes. Like when that meth ring got busted last year, two blocks over. Couple guys involved were undocumented. Started rumors. Made people side-eye every new face. Broke my heart, because most immigrants I know work twice as hard as anyone just to survive. But fear spreads fast when jobs are thin and trust is thinner.

So I guess my feeling is… cautious hope? I want everyone here to belong. But belonging means responsibility too. If you’re part of this garden, you pull weeds. You don’t dump trash. You don’t scare kids. You show up.

And if you do? Then you’re my neighbor. Doesn’t matter where you started.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Yeah… I’ll be honest — not every situation feels natural. But comfort ain’t the point. *Respect* is.

Take Mike, two doors down. Lives with his partner, both men. They’ve got a little boy — adopted, real sweet kid. At first, me and some of the older guys used to joke about it, dumb stuff, what we heard growing up. But then you see them — how they fix their porch every weekend, how they bring food when someone’s sick. You realize they’re just like us — trying to raise a kid safe, keep a roof over his head. So yeah, different? Sure. But they’re *here*, doing right. That earns space.

Same with people struggling — like Linda, who drinks too much sometimes. She’s alone, lost her son in a car wreck. Broke. Doesn’t hurt nobody, but she yells at night, leaves bottles on her stoop. I don’t love it, but I also remember my uncle after Mom passed — he wasn’t mean, just broken. Took time. So we don’t shun her. We check on her. One of the Haitian women from upstairs brings her soup when she’s bad off. That’s tolerance with dignity — not pretending it’s fine, but saying, “You still matter.”

Now, substance abuse — that’s harder. Because it *can* spill over. Like when someone’s shooting up in the stairwell. That ain’t just uncomfortable — it’s dangerous. Kids play here. My niece comes through that door. That’s where tolerance ends and safety begins. Same if someone’s violent or spreading disease and not taking care. I had a cousin die from hepatitis C — started with dirty needles. So yeah, I get why people panic.

But here’s the thing Character05_M always said: *“You deal with the problem, not the person.”* Treat the addict like a human, but lock down the risk. Get them help. Provide clean syringes if it stops disease — not because we approve, but because we protect the rest. Same with TB or HIV — no shame, but responsibility. If you’re sick, you take steps. We help you do it right.

And language? Religion? That’s easy. If you’re praying five times a day, cool. Just don’t block the sidewalk. If you wear a hijab or a cross or nothing at all — fine. But speak *to* people, not just past them. Learn enough English to say “hello,” “thank you,” “my kid needs help.” Not to erase who you are — but to build something *together.*

The big gap? When people live side by side but never talk. Like the Vietnamese family downstairs — been here ten years, barely say a word to anyone. Keep to themselves. Quiet. Polite. But you don’t know if they need help until the pipes burst at 2 a.m. and they’re standing in water, calling nobody.

That’s where communication falls short. Fear goes both ways — they might be scared of us too. Think we’ll judge, report them, make trouble.

So tolerance isn’t just on *our* side. It’s on *all* sides.

We need more of those garden meetings — real ones, not city paperwork. Bring chairs out. Share food. Let kids run. Talk. Not debate politics — just *be* together. That’s how trust grows. Not in speeches. In small things.

Because in the end? We all want the same: safety, respect, a place where your kid can play without fear.

If we start there — instead of differences — most of this stuff works itself out.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character05_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Alright… now we’re talking about the real stuff. The kind that keeps you up at night when the bills are due and the garage cut your hours.

When jobs are thin — *really* thin — fairness, to me, means **first come, first served — but not by birth certificate. By commitment.** If you’ve been here ten years, paying taxes, raising kids, trying to work, you should get first shot at the work going around — doesn’t matter if you were born in Alabama or Angola.

But here’s where it gets raw: I’ve seen guys like me — white, local, high school diploma, no fancy skills — passed over for temp jobs because some contractor brings in a crew from out of state or overseas who’ll work under the table, no benefits, no overtime, half the wage.

That ain’t fair.

Not to us. And honestly? It ain’t fair to them either. Those workers are being used. They’re scared to speak up, scared to get hurt, scared to lose what little they got. That drives wages down for everybody. Now nobody wins.

So balance? Yeah, I want balance. But it can’t be “locals only” and slam the door. That’s not how this country was built. My granddad was Irish — people hated him when he came. Called him names. But he dug ditches, laid brick, raised a family. Earned his place.

Same with folks today. But — and this is big — **they gotta play by the same rules we do.** If we need licenses, they need licenses. If we pay taxes, they pay taxes. If we follow safety rules on the job site, so do they.

No backdoor deals. No “I’ll pay you cash under the table” nonsense that screws the rest of us.

And yeah, I’ll admit — sometimes I get bitter. Like when I see a restaurant fully staffed with guys who don’t speak English, all hired the same week, while my cousin’s been applying everywhere for months. But then I ask: *Are they legal? Are they documented? Are they paying into the system?*

If yes — then fine. Competition’s tough, but that’s life. We all hustle.

If no — then that’s the problem. Not them as people. The *system* letting employers exploit them and undercut us both.

So my answer? Tighten the rules. Make sure everyone’s in the same boat — legally, fairly. Audit the companies hiring off the books. Fine them hard. Stop rewarding greed.

And invest — really invest — in training programs for locals who’ve been left behind. Not just diplomas, but real skills: welding, plumbing, solar tech. Stuff that pays. Give us a chance to *earn* the work, not just whine about losing it.

Because if we fix the game — make it honest — then I don’t fear immigrants. I fear lazy bosses and broken laws.

Fairness isn’t keeping people out. It’s making sure we’re all playing the same damn game.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character05_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Alright… let’s cut through the noise.

I hear all these arguments — on TV, at the garage, over beers — and most of ’em got *some* truth to ’em. But a lot of it’s just fear talking, dressed up like facts.

Let’s go one by one.

**“Immigrants fill jobs nobody else wants.”**  
Yeah… that one’s real. I’ve seen it. Meatpacking plants, farm work, overnight warehouse shifts — hot, dangerous, low pay. A lot of guys like me *say* they’d take it, but when it comes down to it? You don’t see many white kids from my neighborhood lining up for 12-hour days in a chicken plant, breathing feathers and blood mist. So yeah, immigrants do those jobs. And if they didn’t, your grocery bill would double. That’s not opinion — that’s what the guy at the union hall told me. So that part? Reasonable. Solid.

**“They bring culture, food, music — make things more alive.”**  
Sure. I like tacos. I like reggae nights at the park. I like how the halal cart on 5th has the best chicken skewers in town. I ain’t scared of flavor. But let’s be honest — when people say this, they’re usually talking from a distance. They don’t live in the building where the new family’s cooking strong spices and the smoke alarm keeps going off. Or where the language barrier means nobody knows there’s bedbugs until half the floor’s infested. So the *idea* of diversity? Great. The *daily grind* of it? That takes work. Patience. Communication. Most folks aren’t ready for that part.

**“Crime and security risks — we can’t trust everyone.”**  
Now this one… it hits hard. Because I’ve seen bad stuff. That MS-13 thing out east — yeah, some of those kids were undocumented. And the fentanyl? A lot of it’s coming across the border. You can’t just wave that off. But then again — most of the guys I know locked up? Born right here. Grew up three blocks from me. So is it *immigration* causing crime, or poverty, drugs, no hope?

I think people mix up correlation and cause. Just ’cause someone’s foreign-born and in jail doesn’t mean immigration made them criminal. Some are. Most aren’t. I worked with a Guatemalan guy — José — ten years. Never missed a day. Sent money home to his mom every week. Got papers the legal way. Now *that’s* the norm. But you don’t see headlines saying “Immigrant Pays Taxes, Fixes Cars, Mows Lawn.” Doesn’t sell.

So this view? Needs facts. Not fear. We need to know: Are undocumented communities *actually* more violent? Or does it just *feel* that way because we only hear the worst cases? I don’t know for sure. But I think the data says no. My cousin’s a cop — he tells me most of the guys he busts are local. Same as us. Just lost.

**“We have a moral duty — refugees, poor folks, people running for their lives.”**  
Yeah. That gets me. I’m not religious, but I got a heart. If a kid’s fleeing gangs, war, starvation — and we slam the door? That ain’t right. My granddad’s family came in a potato sack almost. Not proud, but true. So I get it.

But here’s my hang-up: **Why do we help people from far away while ignoring our own?**  

I see tents full of homeless vets on the corner. Kids in my old school eating one meal a day. People OD’ing in alleys. And the government’s flying in thousands from halfway across the world — which is good, maybe — but where was that urgency when it was *us* falling apart?

So I don’t hate the humanitarian angle. I just want it to include *everyone*. Don’t save a child from Syria and leave mine freezing on the street.

And finally — **the big one: “They’re taking our jobs and lowering wages.”**  
That one? It cuts deep because… sometimes it’s true. Not always. But *sometimes.* When companies skip hiring locals and bus in crews who can’t complain, can’t unionize, can’t fight back — yeah, that drags wages down. That makes life harder for people like me.

But again — is the problem the worker? Or the boss exploiting both of us?

I’d rather fix the system than blame the guy just trying to survive.

So in the end?  
- I believe in second chances — for refugees, for hard workers.  
- I respect labor — whoever’s doing it, if it’s honest.  
- I fear lawlessness — whether it’s smugglers, gangs, or greedy employers.  
- And I demand fairness — not special treatment for outsiders *or* insiders.

What needs more dialogue? The middle ground. The quiet majority — legal immigrants, struggling locals, mixed neighborhoods — trying to make it work. We don’t hear from them enough.

We need town halls, not Twitter wars. Real talk. Over food. With translators if needed. Because once you sit across from someone, share a meal, hear about their kid’s asthma or how they miss their grandma — it’s harder to hate.

And that’s where it starts. Not with laws. With people.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character05_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t go for any of those extremes — not complete openness, and sure as hell not slamming the door shut. That’s all fantasy talk, either from dreamers or fear-mongers.

What I’d want — what makes sense to me — is a mix: **controlled flow, based on real need, with clear rules and consequences.**

So here’s how I see it.

First — **admit people based on job demand**, but *only* if those jobs can’t be filled locally after a real effort. Not just “we posted it once.” I mean: Work with job centers, train people, give locals first shot. If nobody’s qualified or willing after six weeks? Then bring someone in — but legally, documented, taxed.

And tie that visa to the job. No switching employers without approval. No overstaying. If you lose the job, you don’t just disappear into the shadows — you either find another approved work within a time limit, or you go back. That keeps it fair. No undercutting wages. No exploitation.

Second — **set numerical limits**, yeah, but not some random number pulled outta the air every election year. Base it on data — housing, schools, infrastructure. Can this town handle fifty more families? Then let in fifty. Overwhelmed? Slow it down. Simple. Not cruel. Just practical.

And spread it out. Don’t dump 5,000 people in one city with broken systems. That’s asking for trouble — resentment, strain, failure. Do it region by region, pace by pace.

Third — **protect asylum, but process it fast and fair.** If someone’s running from war, violence, death threats — we can’t turn them away cold. But right now, the system’s a joke. People wait years in limbo. Others abuse it, showing up with fake stories just to get a foothold. So fix it: Hire more judges, speed up hearings, cut the backlog. Approve real cases quick. Send back the frauds. No games.

And while they’re waiting? They work — low-level jobs, community service, whatever. Not locked up. Not on full benefits. But not sitting idle, either. Earn your keep while you make your case.

Fourth — **zero tolerance for illegal entry and hiring.** Seal the damn border — not with a wall, maybe, but with tech, patrols, and real consequences. And punish the *employers* who hire under the table. Fine them heavy. Shut them down. Because that’s what breaks trust — knowing some boss can break the rules and profit while the rest of us play fair.

And finally — **integration isn’t optional.**  
Newcomers get six months to learn basic English. Not fluent — just enough to function. Take a civics class. Learn the laws, the values, how things work here. Pass a test. Then apply for residency. No permanent guests. If you can’t or won’t, then this ain’t the place for you.

Same goes for communities — we’ve got to step up too. Not just expect immigrants to adapt. We gotta meet them halfway. Say hello. Offer help. Share space.

Because policy ain’t just about borders and visas. It’s about what happens *after*. Can you rent an apartment? Get your kid in school? Feel safe walking outside?

A fair system doesn’t promise easy — but it promises *clear.* You know the rules. You follow them. You earn your place.

That’s the kind of policy I’d back: tough but fair. Practical, not punishing. Open to workers and refugees — but rooted in order, honesty, and shared responsibility.

Not blind openness. Not closed fists.

Just… a working door. With a lock. And a key you have to earn.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character05_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character05_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…Yeah. I did.

I mean — I thought I knew him well. We went back years. But doing this, really stepping into his voice like that… it wasn’t just repeating what he said. It was feeling *why* he said it.

Before, when he talked about immigrants taking jobs or wages going down, I used to hear anger. Like maybe he was bitter, even a little racist sometimes. But sitting here today, trying to speak as him — I realized it wasn’t about race at all. It was about dignity. About fairness in the dirt, where you live paycheck to paycheck and every small loss feels like a fall.

He wasn’t scared of people from other countries. He was scared of being forgotten. Of working hard and still getting pushed aside — not by immigrants, really, but by a system that sees all of us regular folks as disposable.

And the deeper we went, the more I saw how much he actually *respected* people who came here and tried — legally, honestly. He didn’t resent their struggle. He resented that *his* struggle never got the same recognition.

That hit me.

And honestly? It made me rethink my own views. I’ve always leaned more open, more welcoming — which I still believe in. But I never fully understood the tension on the ground — how fast trust breaks when people feel replaced instead of joined.

It’s easy for me to say “be kind, be open” when I’ve got a degree, a stable job, options. But for him? Every decision felt like survival. Not fear-mongering — just realism with scars.

This conversation made me see that compassion has to go both ways. We can’t welcome others while ignoring the pain of our own poor, our own left-behind towns and broken schools. That breeds division. And the powerful? They love that. Keep us fighting each other while they make the rules.

So now I think: real fairness means lifting *everyone* — newcomers and locals alike — not playing one against the other.

And maybe that’s what Character05_M really wanted all along — not walls, not handouts, but a fair field. Where effort matters more than where you started.

I miss him. But today, for a little while, it felt like he was right here — not shouting, not angry, just talking plain truth from the heart.

And that… that changed something in me.
